idiom_name: one metadata field + closed token vocabulary + token-to-deserialiser registry + routing rule on the same field
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: agree on one metadata field name and a closed vocabulary of token values; the producer sets the token in the same step that serialises the body; the consumer reads the token, looks it up in a registry of deserialisers and parses the body exactly once with the matching one; routers, selectors and filters reference that same field so no component needs the payload. The classic structure is always justified when the transport offers no metadata section - then the hint must live in a wrapper inside the payload, which is the content-based sibling.
code_sketch:
produce: header["type"] = "order-created"; send(header, encode(body))
consume: token  = msg.header("type")
         reader = registry[token]        # closed allowlist; missing key => reject
         event  = reader(msg.body)       # body parsed once, by the right parser
route:   broker.rule("type = 'order-created'")   # metadata only, body untouched
pitfalls: Token and body are written in two places; if they can drift, the receiver silently deserialises the wrong type.
A metadata channel that is not preserved end to end (bridges, archives, header-stripping consumers) loses the hint.
An open registry keyed by sender-supplied class or type names is a remote type-selection hole.
Using a framework class name or assembly name as a sender-controlled token exposes unsafe polymorphic deserialization; use stable registry ids and an allowlist instead.
Treating a missing type header as permission to use a silent default class hides producer/consumer drift; reject it or make the compatibility policy explicit.
